title: Elf Name Generator
description: Elf names in three styles: real elves from Tolkien's books, D&D-style names, and original fantasy names. Male, female and gender-neutral.

hero.title: 🧝 Elf Name Generator
hero.tagline: Elves from Tolkien's books, D&D-style names and original fantasy names: pick a style and go.

article.intro: Elf names have a sound you recognise straight away: soft consonants, long vowels and endings like -iel, -wen and -ion. This **elf name generator** gives you three takes on it. Tolkien gives you real elves from Middle-earth, D&D gives you names in the style of the Player's Handbook, and Generic gives you original names that don't belong to any one world.

sections.heading: Tolkien's elves: names with meanings
sections.content:
Every name in the Tolkien style is an elf from Tolkien's books, and almost all of them mean something in his Elvish languages, Sindarin and Quenya:

  • Legolas: "green leaves" (Sindarin)
  • Elrond: "star-dome"
  • Arwen: "noble maiden"
  • Celebrían: "silver queen"
  • Círdan: "shipwright", fitting for the elf who builds the ships to the West
  • Gil-galad: "star of radiance"
  • Fëanor: "spirit of fire"

Because they're real characters, fans will recognise them. That's perfect for a Middle-earth game or an elf named after a hero of old. For an original character, borrow the building blocks instead (below).

sections.heading: Build your own Tolkien-style elf name
sections.content:
Tolkien built his names from real word parts, and you can do the same:

  • gil star, galad radiance, celeb silver, mith grey, nim white
  • -wen maiden and -iel daughter, for female names (Arwen, Eärwen "sea-maiden", Galadriel)
  • -ion son, and -dil friend or lover (Eärendil, "friend of the sea")
  • -dor land, for names tied to a place

So Celebwen reads as "silver maiden" and Mithion as "grey son". Neither is in the books, but both feel at home there, and you'll know what they mean.

sections.heading: D&D elves: child names, adult names and family names
sections.content:
In Dungeons & Dragons (5th edition), elves go by a child name until they declare themselves adults, sometime after their hundredth birthday, and then choose an adult name. That's a nice detail for a character: a young elf might still be using a short child name, or be about to pick a new one.

D&D elf family names usually come with a translation, which you can use in Common: Galanodel (Moonwhisper), Liadon (Silverfrond), Holimion (Diamonddew). If you give your elf a family name, deciding what it means in Common gives other characters something to call them.

The D&D style here sounds like the Player's Handbook: flowing, with ae, ai and th, like Aelthas, Faenya and Saelvan. A few, like Naivara and Shanairra, are names the Player's Handbook itself suggests. The gender-neutral D&D names are short (Aeris, Faen, Rael), which suits child names well.

sections.heading: Generic elf names
sections.content:
The generic style is for elves outside any particular world. Male names tend to end in -ion, -or or -as (Ithilion, Calenor), female names in -iel, -wen or -a (Ariniel, Elowen, Talindra).

Gender-neutral generic names are nature words: Willow, Rowan, Wren, Briar, Ember. They work well for wood elves, druids or an elf who's taken a name in the common tongue.

Looking for a Christmas elf rather than a Tolkien one? Try the Elf on the Shelf and Christmas Elf name generators.

faqs.question: Are the Tolkien names real?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every name in the Tolkien style is an elf from Tolkien's books (The Hobbit, The Lord of the Rings and The Silmarillion). Use them for Middle-earth games or homages; for an original character, borrow Tolkien's word parts instead.

faqs.question: What's the difference between the three styles?
faqs.answer: Tolkien gives you real Middle-earth elves with meanings in Sindarin and Quenya. D&D gives you names in the style of the Player's Handbook, with ae/ai sounds and family names that translate into Common. Generic gives you original elvish-sounding names that suit any setting.

faqs.question: How are male and female elf names different?
faqs.answer: Mostly in the endings. Female names often end in -iel, -wen or -a; male names in -ion, -or, -as or a consonant. The gender-neutral names avoid those endings, using short names or nature words instead.

faqs.question: Can I use a Tolkien name for my D&D elf?
faqs.answer: In your own game, absolutely. If you're writing something to publish, invent your own name: the famous ones are too recognisable, and Tolkien's word parts give you plenty to work with.
